notes.text: The forward lines keep changing. Even their four most-used trios over the last 10 games cover only 28% of their forwards’ 5-on-5 time, the third-lowest in the league (a typical team: 40%). The lines listed lean on their latest games, but expect new combinations tonight.
Filip Chytil is on injured reserve (upper-body injury) and has missed the last 2 games. He is one of their most valuable skaters.
Tom Willander is day to day (lower-body injury) and missed their last game. He is a top-four defenseman. Zeev Buium has taken his spot beside Jamie Oleksiak.
Jacob Quillan was added to the roster on Oct 31 and has played beside Linus Karlsson and Liam Öhgren.
Max Sasson has started killing penalties: on the ice for 30% of the team’s shorthanded time in 17 games, up from 4% last season.

They dressed 11 forwards and 7 defensemen in 3 of their last 10 games, including the last one. Morgan Barron takes shifts on two lines, L3 and L4. Tyrel Bauer is the seventh defenseman, rotating in mostly beside DeMelo and Ferraro.

Josh Morrissey is on injured reserve (wrist injury) and has missed the last 12 games. He is a top-four defenseman. Mario Ferraro has taken his spot beside Dylan DeMelo. That pair has had 48% of the chances at 5-on-5 in 91:40 together, down from 61% with Morrissey.
Nico Daws joined from NJD on Oct 24.
Dawson Mercer joined from NJD on Oct 24 and has played beside Kyle Connor and Viggo Björck.
Jack St. Ivany is no longer killing penalties: 0% of the team’s shorthanded time in 4 games, down from 35% with his old team last season.

stakes: The Canucks go in eighth in the Pacific with 7 points, the Jets seventh in the Central with 13 points.

WPG.head: The Jets have a lot going for them
WPG.body: Even though Winnipeg will be without Morrissey, the Jets have been out-chancing opponents by a wide margin lately and have home-ice advantage. The Canucks can make it interesting if they get good looks.

VAN.head: The Canucks have a hill to climb
VAN.body: Even though Winnipeg will be without Morrissey, the Jets have been out-chancing opponents by a wide margin lately and have home-ice advantage. The Canucks’ best way through is getting good looks.

story.head: Somebody has to win
paras: The Jets (5-8-3) beat Montréal 5-4 in overtime on Tuesday, while the Canucks are on a three-game losing streak. Both teams are near the bottom of the standings. Going in, the Canucks are last in the NHL and the Jets seventh in the Central (26th in the NHL).

The Canucks haven’t played well, but their record (.206) is worse than their play: their chances are worth about .330, mostly because they’re 2-5 in one-goal games. The Jets’ record (.406) is about what their chances are worth.

The Canucks pick their shots (lowest), have had shaky goaltending (32nd) and have a leaky penalty kill (32nd). Vancouver has allowed 4.53 goals a game, the most in the league. As for the Jets, they create more chances on the penalty kill than almost anyone (2nd) and rarely ice the puck (5th), but don't block many shots (28th). Winnipeg has scored 2.44 goals a game, the fourth fewest in the league, and allowed 3.62, the fourth most. The Canucks have the edge over the Jets on depth.

Elias Pettersson (#40) (4 G / 14 A / 18 P in 17 GP) leads the Canucks in scoring, and Jonathan Lekkerimäki (6 G / 7 A / 13 P in 17 GP) has a team-high six goals. For the Jets, Kyle Connor (13 G / 4 A / 17 P in 16 GP) leads the way in scoring, with five goals in eight games against Vancouver since 2023-24. Mark Scheifele (2 G / 12 A / 14 P in 16 GP) isn’t far behind.
Leevi Meriläinen (2-5-1 / .897 SV% in 9 GS) is expected to start for Vancouver, and Stuart Skinner (4-4-3 / .882 SV% in 11 GS) for Winnipeg.
